cards.title: Test SMS/email send frequency with a holdout to prove incrementality
cards.summary: Design a cohort split (normal / zero / double) to measure whether extra messages actually lift revenue before scaling budget.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to increase lifecycle message cadence or justify a growing SMS bill to leadership.
steps: Split your subscriber base into three cohorts: hold steady at current cadence (for example 50%), send nothing at all (for example 25%), and send double the cadence (for example 25%).
Run for a full cycle long enough to capture conversion behavior—Postscript's test moved brands from roughly one text per week to two.
Compare revenue per subscriber across cohorts against the true holdout, not just platform-attributed revenue, to see incremental lift.
If 2x shows a statistically significant revenue lift over holdout, raise cadence; if not, keep the baseline.
Note that in the test described, more sending produced higher ROI with ~98% confidence the 2x group yielded significantly more revenue—treat this as one brand's result, not a universal benchmark.
caveats: Every SMS has a real per-message cost, unlike email, so incremental revenue must clear the toll.
Attribution tools report what happened; only a holdout shows what would have happened otherwise.

cards.title: Set an SMS frequency baseline using subscriber LTV and unsub rate
cards.summary: Use subscriber LTV (acquisition rate, messages per subscriber, revenue per message, unsub rate) to find the send cadence that maximizes revenue without spiking unsubscribes.
cards.use_when: Setting or revising monthly SMS cadence and worried about annoying the list.
steps: Track four metrics: % of list subscribing (acquisition rate), messages sent per subscriber per month, revenue per message, and unsubscribe rate.
Watch unsubscribes inside the first 30 days as the key signal of over-messaging.
Start near Postscript's observed sweet spot of roughly 8–10 texts per subscriber per month, which they report generates high returns with essentially zero impact on baseline unsub rate.
Do not assume this is fixed—the correct baseline must be tested per brand by mapping the relationship between messages per subscriber, revenue, and unsub rate.
Use the data, not gut fear of 'annoying people'—if frequency were a problem, it would surface in the unsub metric.
Recognize real spread across brands: some large brands send ~2 texts/subscriber (e.g., a subscription-first model), while others (e.g., Grüns) send ~20+ in the first 30–45 days.
caveats: 8–10/month is Postscript's observed range, not a guaranteed optimum for every store.
High-frequency brands often accept higher spend for a specific goal such as converting to subscription; low-frequency brands may be filtering out long-term non-buyers to avoid fees.

cards.title: Treat SMS as an acquisition channel, not just retention
cards.summary: Most people who give you a phone number haven't bought yet, so SMS flows are the welcome mat for paid traffic—manage and optimize them like performance marketing.
cards.use_when: Allocating team ownership, budget, or optimization effort across paid acquisition and lifecycle channels.
steps: Recognize that the first action a Meta/Google click often triggers is the signup popup—so SMS/email pop-ups and welcome flows are part of the acquisition funnel.

Track that roughly 25% of compliant double-opt-in subscribers buy within 30 days (Postscript's cross-brand figure); the remaining ~75% are unconverted subscribers whose first-purchase objections still need handling.
Treat the pop-up → welcome series as your acquisition engine, distinct from campaigns that serve retention at day 15/30/45.
Align org structure so one leader sees paid, creative, ecom, and retention—Postscript and operators report that siloed teams miss second-order effects (e.g., an ad change tanking SMS list growth).
Test pop-up changes against full-site conversion rate, not just opt-in rate, because a pop-up can lift signups while hurting checkout.
An operator predicts retention will become the next frontier as paid channels saturate—an opinion, not a guarantee.
caveats: The 25% figure is an aggregate across Postscript's ~25,000 brands, not a target for your store.
Centralizing teams is a recommendation from practitioners, not a proven universal structure.

cards.title: Add a question to lifecycle flows to start conversations
cards.summary: The lowest-effort entry to conversational commerce is appending a simple question to an existing flow message and reading the replies.
cards.use_when: Starting conversational commerce or sourcing zero-party data without new tooling.
steps: Pick any existing flow (welcome series, abandoned cart, delivery follow-up).
After the standard link or message, append a plain question such as 'Is there anything else I can help you with today?' or 'Do you have any questions I can answer?'

Test it: one operator split a 6-message welcome flow, with the variant ending in a question, and it performed well; keep the standard flow to convert the easy 25% then use the question to catch marginal prospects where conversation is required.
Expect volume—operators report brands getting thousands of replies in the first week when they ask.
Mine the replies for objection themes and use them to guide future flows and ad copy.
Extend this to more touchpoints: post-delivery usage questions, winback, long-consideration prospects.
caveats: For short-consideration, low-ticket impulse buys (e.g., a wallet before Father's Day), conversation at the end of the flow is sufficient—going conversation-first is overkill.
For long-consideration or high-ticket categories (e.g., a $1,000 sofa with a ~90-day window), consider putting conversation earlier to compress the decision.

cards.title: Match conversation strategy to consideration period and ticket size
cards.summary: When and how aggressively to open conversations depends on how long buyers deliberate and how high the stakes are.
cards.use_when: Designing whether flows should lead with conversation or stay broadcast-first for a given product category.
steps: Identify your category's consideration period (time from click/opt-in to purchase).
For short, impulse-driven buys, run a normal broadcast flow and reserve conversation for the end to handle stragglers.
For long-consideration or high-ticket items, place conversation earlier—the source compares it to putting your best salesperson in front of a shopper while they compare you to competitors.
For one-time-to-subscription conversion, which carries an outsized value bump, lean conversation-heavy to handle objections and upsell.
Use winback and unconverted-senior-subscriber segments as conversation targets, since they've engaged with texts but never bought.
Post-delivery, ask a follow-up question about product usage to open a dialogue at the best moment for repeat purchase.
caveats: Consideration-period length is a judgment call per category; the source gives 90 days as an example for furniture, not a rule.

cards.title: Use conversation data to build real zero-party customer attributes
cards.summary: Conversations surface static facts and ephemeral attributes you can operationalize across text and your CDP.
cards.use_when: Enriching subscriber profiles with personalization data and building one-to-one messaging.
steps: Instrument conversational replies so the content is queryable, not just answered in the moment.
Separate static data (a purchase made a year ago, a SKU, a subscription tier) from ephemeral data that changes over time (a child ages from 1 to 2, seasonal location, a fitness or health change).
Push attributes into your CRM/CDP so they can inform messaging beyond SMS—the source is building toward API/MCP access so personas like Claude can consume them (verify current availability).
Build triggers around ephemeral attributes: a daughter's next birthday, a season change, a size change after a weight-loss journey.
Treat this as the path to 'audience of one' personalization marketers have chased but lacked data to execute.

Example of the kind of data conversations yield: a belt brand learned a wife buys for her husband, that he was on a health journey down 40 lbs, and that his size would keep changing—actionable but not obtainable from browsing data alone.
Operators report subscribers who have a conversation with the brand show ~1.5x higher lifetime value—an internal metric, not a guarantee.
caveats: Postscript's API/MCP access was in development at the recording—check current product docs.
The 1.5x LTV lift is the vendor's observed metric; validate on your own list.

cards.title: Use SMS/MMS/RCS as distinct channels and enable RCS for richer actions
cards.summary: RCS is a separate messaging channel with SMS fallback that raises the creative ceiling with carousels, video, and native action buttons.
cards.use_when: Planning SMS creative formats and considering RCS rollouts for launches or drops.
steps: Understand RCS is not SMS/MMS—it's its own protocol; if a recipient can't receive RCS, messages fall back to SMS in tools like Postscript.
Use RCS for rich formats: carousel scrolling, video, and native action buttons.
For product drops, use the iOS calendar action button so recipients can add a launch date directly instead of a vague 'watch this space' text.
Exploit native CTAs that integrate with the phone to expand use cases on the messaging channel.
Operators report outsized performance on RCS over SMS/MMS—treat as early directional signal, not a benchmark.
Confirm current carrier/device support and platform interface before committing budget, as RCS availability and features change.
caveats: RCS performance claims are early-stage and vendor-reported.
Feature availability (e.g., iOS calendar) varies by platform and time—verify in your messaging tool.

cards.title: Adapt to customer data through conversations
cards.summary: Persistent conversations uncover the objections preventing purchase that no PDP can pre-empt, so build a process to capture and act on those objections.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing mid-funnel purchase blockers and reducing friction at PDP and checkout.
steps: Run ongoing conversations on your list to capture live objections people don't broadcast anywhere else.

Look for objections that are too specific to design for: e.g., a shopper who would only buy 'Miracle Balm' if assured it holds up to a 5-hour-a-day gardening/sweating regimen, or a buyer whose cart total ($75) exceeded her budget ($68) and who needed a small offer to close.
Use conversational tools to handle these at the moment of decision (the source's Shopper AI handles shade-matching and small price-gap offers automatically).
Query conversation archives to surface trends and recurring blockers (the source's 'Ask Shopper' feature).
Feed the discovered objections back into PDP copy, FAQ, and ad creative so future traffic self-serves.
Treat conversation logs as arguably your richest consumer-insight stream, since many brands never text customers at all.
caveats: The specific brand examples (Jones Road, belts) are illustrative, not benchmarks.
Automated handling of price-gap offers requires merchant-defined guardrails—set them deliberately.

cards.title: Chase incremental value in retention channels as paid channels saturate
cards.summary: As the curve of paid acquisition flattens, finer optimization of lifecycle messaging on owned channels becomes the marginal growth lever.
cards.use_when: Setting next-quarter growth priorities and allocating between paid acquisition and lifecycle optimization.
steps: Recognize that as paid opportunities are exhausted, marginal value moves into retention channels—the source quotes a CMO predicting retention would become the topic of focus after everybody exhausts paid incrementality.
Shift toward precise optimization: for example, deciding whether 50K, 75K, or 100K of monthly SMS spend is most efficient at the margin, not just whether the current spend works.
Scrutinize the SMS bill as a meaningful cost that lives between SaaS costs and performance marketing on the P&L—as it scales, so should the demand for incrementality evidence.
Partner with a vendor or team willing to 'grade their own homework' with holdouts on large spend.
Separate lead conversion (subscribing) from purchase conversion (buying) and from close rate—holdouts and cohort measurement track whether the channel produced net-new purchases.
caveats: The CMO's retention prediction is a forecast, not a law.
Retention-only isn't universal—brands with long consideration periods should still invest in top-of-funnel acquisition.

cards.title: Align pop-ups, flows, and campaigns to the true purchase decision
cards.summary: Pop-ups and welcome flows are acquisition touch points; campaigns are retention—design and own them accordingly.
cards.use_when: Deciding ownership and testing scope for pop-ups, welcome series, and campaigns.
steps: Treat the pop-up and welcome flow as part of the acquisition engine (ad → lander → pop-up → flow), because that chain is the first interaction with many paid visitors.
Treat campaigns as a retention touchpoint where you speak to subscribers at day 15/30/45 with launches and first-party-data-driven messages.
Ensure at least one leader sees both the flow and site behavior so signals aren't missed—e.g., an ad change lowering SMS list growth below forecast.
Test pop-up experience against full-site conversion rate, not just opt-in rate, to catch changes that hurt checkout.
Recognize the 'customer journey as a line' is misleading—people interact with all touchpoints in non-linear ways, so siloed assembly-line thinking invalidates decisions.
Follow the source's 'just ask' rule: solicit conversations at the acquisition stage to intercept people who look like a converted customer but have a first-purchase objection.
caveats: Full-site A/B testing of pop-ups requires sufficient traffic to detect conversion-rate impact.
Org restructuring is contextual—not every store can centralize teams.

input.text:
14-EML / email and lifecycle

Goes here. Klaviyo email system architecture, list growth strategies, high-converting signup forms (pop-ups, full-page, micro-commitments), automated core email flows, email campaign calendar planning, list segmentation, deliverability optimization, and SMS marketing strategy (list growth, flows, campaigns, segmentation, conversational commerce).

Not here.

Paid ad campaign setup, tracking pixels, or Meta Conversions API -> 11-ADC

Evaluating marketing or website analytics -> 06-MEA

25% of people who give you their phone number and buy something in the first 30 days. That's why people keep putting money into the SMS ATM. People are always like, "Oh, I don't want to annoy people." Like, well, if you annoyed people, it would show up as unsub rate, right? You can send about eight messages per person per month and without seeing an uptick in that whatsoever. >> We are in the very early innings of thinking about frequency. >> I really want to test it. Maybe not as aggressive, but I am super curious to test a more elaborate aggressive onboarding experience. >> Well, we'll jump into it. So for those listening, we're obviously here with my Mike Mannheimr. Mike, you're CMO at Postcript or also CMO and chief customer officer. >> Yeah, I I I'm technically I just go by chief customer officer now. >> Got it. >> Um I started at Postcript 5 years ago as the CMO. Um eventually it made sense to take over the customerf facing teams. Um I'm a marketer. We sell to marketers and service marketing teams. And so there's some some crossover there. And so um about 2 years ago I took over the customer side which would be customer success, professional services, onboarding and added that to my existing uh responsibilities on you know marketing and business development. And so all of that reports up to me. And so if you are a postcript customer, thank you very much. You probably have worked with my team. Um if you are not a Postgrip customer, you have probably heard from my team, the other part of my team. And so, um, yeah, that's that's my role at HostGrip. So, technically CCNA. >> Before we get any further into the episode, I want to thank our sponsors as always, Motion, Preient, Rich Panel, After Cell, and House. Motion just dropped their 2026 creative benchmarks report, and it's been getting shared everywhere. Slack channels, LinkedIn, Twitter, sharing it in our private group chats. And it's great because everybody's been asking the same four questions forever. What is normal? How many ads should we actually be shipping? What is a healthy hit rate? And which formats really win? The report analyzes over 575,000 creatives from 6,000 advertisers in over a billion dollars in ad spend to answer these exact questions. And the report has some really interesting findings like the fact that only 4 to 8% of ads actually become winners and over half of ads actually lose. And for motion customers, this report is especially helpful. You can upload it into your motion dashboard with their runth AI chat and compare it directly against your vertical benchmarks. Hit the link in the show notes. I promise you won't regret it. And as always, go to motionapp.com and tell the marketing operator sent you. I wanted to start with actually Cody and I are contra contractually obligated to discuss incrementality on every episode. Um so so we're going to start with incrementality and hold out testing in SMS. Um because I was thinking about this a little bit more. This is this is um you know I hear this said all the time. People regret not sending more emails. >> Uh-huh. This is this is one of those things like it is advice. I'm sure there are a lot of people out there that aren't technically sending enough emails, but like everybody on DTOC Twitter has learned this lesson. It's just like it's one of those things where it's like it's said and it sounds like good advice, but everybody immediately agrees. So, it's just kind of like a good take to throw out there every once in a while. What what I want to talk about is how that relates to SMS because I feel like we are in the very early innings of thinking about frequency and therefore the incrementality of SMS. So I was just curious for you to talk through what's postcripts POV on like just SMS volume. Are there best practices? I know you guys kind of pioneered the subscriber LTV metric.
